title: Opening Words - Being AI-Native Relevant - The Hobby Way

speakers.name: Gadi Evron
speakers.affiliation: CEO and Co-founder, Knostic; CISO-in-Residence for AI, CSA; Chair, [un]prompted conference

thesis: Defenders should stop automating their existing workflows faster and instead restructure security work around what models do natively, using vulnerability research, application security and threat intelligence as three worked examples. The attackers' singularity moment has already happened and the defenders' has to follow.
summary: Gadi Evron opens day 3 by recapping the previous day's demos and then walking through three of his own personal projects as examples of staying relevant with AI. He recaps a Doom demo where a live function was rewritten with a model so monsters stopped firing, and a second demo where a simple web app detected a SQL injection in its logs and patched the vulnerable function on the fly, which he calls purely vibe coded and not production ready. He then introduces a four-layer model of AI usage (automate yourself, orchestrate the automation, structure data natively for the model, AI-native), says attackers mostly work at layers one to three and rarely at layer four (AI-native), and describes his hunt for logic vulnerabilities. He says that led to Snouter, a symmetry and asymmetry mapper, which he reports found over 600 results on Raptor and helped surface an OpenBMC IPMI privilege escalation with HD Moore. A later graph tool, Code Surf, maps relationships among values, call sites, routes and trust zones rather than source-to-sink flows. He reports that running it on Raptor gave 2,500 findings but one defense-in-depth bug, so he reused the findings as a dataset to map which guards each finding shape passes through, and proposes watching guard coverage regressions instead of chasing patches. Last, he presents Adversary Brains, a threat intelligence approach that scales analysis of competing hypotheses to thousands of weighted hypotheses used as detection signatures, published as an arXiv preprint. He closes with a call to try ideas that fail, retry with each new model, and take AI back from the marketers.
argument: Attackers have already moved to automating and orchestrating with AI, and defenders need their own step change rather than faster versions of current work.
AI usage has four layers (automate yourself, orchestrate the automation, structure data natively for the model, and AI-native), and security work rarely reaches the fourth.
Asking models for unnamed logic flaws led through symmetry and asymmetry mapping and a relationship graph of code to results that classic source-to-sink tools do not surface.

Because endless vulnerability findings cannot all be patched, the findings can be reused as a dataset to map which guards protect which flows, so defenders maintain a few thousand guards and watch for regressions.
The same shift applies to threat intelligence: instead of IOCs and prose reports, keep operational hypothesis graphs (adversary brains) that match arrangements of evidence and name the missing links.
Practitioners should try ideas that do not work, retry them on each new model, prioritise recall over benchmarks at first, then productionise.

claims.claim: A web app can detect a SQL injection in its own logs and patch the vulnerable function live so the same attack fails on the second attempt.
claims.evidence: Demo 2 on an intentionally simple web app: the first injection worked, the repeat failed. The slide shows a critical SQL injection incident on app.main:search marked fixed, with the function rewritten and live. Evron calls it purely vibe coded and not necessarily production ready.

claims.claim: A running function in a game can be replaced live by describing the desired behavior to a model, here making Doom monsters stop firing and walk toward the player.
claims.evidence: Demo 1 recap. The failed live run the day before is acknowledged. The slide shows a controller UI proposing candidate functions (decideMonster, decideMonsters) from 254 functions.

claims.claim: Offensive AI use is mostly at layers 1 to 3 of a four-layer model, and rarely at layer 4, AI-native.
claims.evidence: His own model of AI usage and his assessment of attack practice; the slide marks layers 1 to 3 YES and layer 4 RARELY. No data given.

claims.claim: A symmetry and asymmetry mapper (Snouter) turned up over 600 results on Raptor, a project built by strong vulnerability researchers.
claims.evidence: Stated as a first-run result. Not verified or triaged; he says the goal was code smells and leads, not verification at that stage.

claims.claim: The symmetry approach helped lead to a CVE in OpenBMC IPMI after HD Moore, who had worked on OpenBMC for about three months, sent it as an exhausted target.
claims.evidence: Slide shows CVE-2026-16140, OpenBMC IPMI Privilege Escalation via Retargeted RAKP 1, a logic flaw in phosphor-net-ipmid (CWE-863), published 2026-09-15 by runZero, credits HD Moore and Gadi Evron as finders and Tod Beardsley as coordinator.

claims.claim: Docstring or contract versus code comparison done semantically by a model is an AI-native (layer 3) way to find bugs, with no instructions needed for some newer models.
claims.evidence: Described as a worked idea, with two colleagues taking it further; no results given.

claims.claim: Starting with a newer Opus model, asking the model to map trust boundaries works better than describing source-to-sink flows.
claims.evidence: Credited to a colleague's suggestion (Kat Traxler on the slide) and described as working; no quantitative comparison.

claims.claim: Code Surf, a graph abstraction over relationships among values, call sites, routes and trust zones, finds structural shapes such as bypass diamonds, guard splits and cross-zone cycles that existing tools miss or present oddly.
claims.evidence: Slides define a shape as a relationship among mapped values, call sites, routes, trust zones or conditions, and show the cross-zone-cycle shape (v0.3.0, tier T5, cycle). No hit rates shown.

claims.claim: Running the tool on Raptor produced 2,500 findings but only one defense-in-depth bug, which Raptor's hardening explains.
claims.evidence: Stated figure and slide text; the project is well hardened by the speaker's account.

claims.claim: Findings can be reused as a dataset to map which guards each finding shape passes through, so that defenders track a few thousand guards instead of an unbounded stream of vulnerabilities, and watch for guard coverage regressions.
claims.evidence: A Sankey diagram of finding shapes to guards to sinks on Raptor, including a NO GUARD row. Evron says he does not know whether it will scale.

claims.claim: Adversary brains, weighted hypothesis graphs scored against observations across time and systems, can act as detection signatures like YARA and Sigma and flag the missing link when an adversary shifts infrastructure.
claims.evidence: Conceptual slides (YARA matches a file, Sigma matches a log line, a brain matches an arrangement; known unknown to known flow) and an arXiv preprint. No detection results presented in the talk.

claims.claim: Analysis of competing hypotheses, traditionally capped at a handful of hypotheses, can be scaled to thousands with LLMs.
claims.evidence: Asserted; the original write-up's limit of seven is cited from memory with a comment that decision makers should get two to four.

frameworks.name: Four Layers to AI Usage
frameworks.description: Layer 1: automate and orchestrate ourselves. Layer 2: automate and orchestrate layer 1, then again, up to N. Layer 3: structure data natively for the model, or have it read data natively. Layer 4: AI-native. For attack he rates 1 to 3 as common and 4 as rare.

frameworks.name: Code Surf shapes
frameworks.description: A code surf shape is a relationship among mapped values, call sites, routes, trust zones or conditions, or a ranking of such relationships. Examples shown: bypass diamond, guard split, cross-zone cycle (data that loops across a trust boundary and back).

frameworks.name: Symmetry and asymmetry mapping (Snouter)
frameworks.description: Look for missing symmetry, such as three of four sibling functions having a check, or a docstring that does not semantically match its function, as leads for logic flaws.

frameworks.name: Guard coverage regression (AppSec is now Ops)
frameworks.description: Map finding shapes to the guards they pass through and onto sinks; track which guards carry the most and which shapes rest on one guard; alert when a shape loses a guard.

frameworks.name: Adversary Brains
frameworks.description: Hypothesis-based logical signatures for threat actor detection: weighted, related observations scored across time and systems, which can be split, merged, retired or faded, used like YARA and Sigma rules, and read backwards to turn a half-matched brain into a collection task.

artifacts.name: Adversary Brains: Hypothesis-Based Logical Signatures for Threat Actor Detection with LLMs

slide_only: Title slide lists Evron as CEO and Co-founder of Knostic, CISO-in-Residence for AI at CSA, and Chair of the [un]prompted conference.
The speaker credits the trust boundary idea to Kat Traxler (spelled that way on the slide; the transcript garbles it).
The behavior gadget chains slide points to a talk by Daniel Geyshis and Tamir Isaschar on BITE for malicious MCP discovery and false positives.
Doom demo UI shows the model used as claude-haiku-5-5, 5467 ms, three candidates, looked at 120 of 254 functions, with decideMonster and decideMonsters proposed.

Self-healing demo UI shows a banner SQL injection - critical, Automatic binding created: app.main:search rewritten and bound on authz/dev, one incident fixed 7 seconds earlier, and a live call with input q=' UNION SELECT id, body, project FROM docs -- returning empty results; the app runs on CPython 3.12.13.

Sankey slide guard names: path_confine, safe_env, safe_extract, git_safe_cmd, sandbox_run, url_allowlist, safe_load, import_allowlist, param_query, log_escape. Sinks: archive extract, subprocess, file write, HTTP out, deserialise, dynamic import, database, terminal.

Sankey slide finding shapes include bundle upload to tar extract (sink-reach) with NO GUARD, artifact zip to unpack, PATH to tool runner, repo name to git clone (guard-split), run_tool() (chokepoint), webhook URL to HTTP fetch, config file to YAML load, plugin name to import, search term to SQL, log line to terminal.
Cross-zone-cycle slide: version v0.3.0, tier T5, kind cycle, identity variant with members (set) = nodes; zones are outside input, app, privileged sinks; example nodes queue, on_msg(), reply().

Adversary brain comparison slide: a YARA rule matches a file (one artifact judged on its own bytes); a Sigma rule matches a log line (one event, with correlations to join a few); an adversary brain matches the arrangement (many observations, weighted and related, across time and systems).
Cluster slide shows known campaigns APT-A and APT-B, an emergent unnamed cluster, noise, and a new incident point.

From unknown to known slide: unknown activity fits no brain; known unknown is a new value filling a pattern slot or one step stopping matching while the rest holds; known is when collection finds the missing evidence or rules it out. Run backwards, a half-finished brain names the evidence worth searching for, and a filter becomes a collection task.
Closing slide: The Hackening, Take AI back from the marketers, attributed to Gadi Evron.
demos: Doom recap: a model-driven rewrite of the monster decision function in a running game, shown on slides as the in-place-ai controller listing candidate functions; the monsters stopped firing and walked toward the player. The live attempt the previous day failed.

Self-healing SQL injection: a simple search web app was hit with a SQL injection that worked, the attack was detected in the log, the search function was rewritten and bound live, and the repeat attack failed.

quotes.text: The attackers' singularity moment already happened. Now it's time for ours.
quotes.speaker: Gadi Evron

quotes.text: If SAST or fuzzing can find it, if it can be shown in threat modelling, if it has a name, I don't want it.
quotes.speaker: Gadi Evron

quotes.speaker: Gadi Evron

offense: Asking a model to find logic flaws that SAST, fuzzing and threat modeling would not name, via symmetry and asymmetry between sibling functions and between docstrings and code.
Graph-based shapes of code behavior (bypass diamond, guard split, cross-zone cycle) as leads rather than verified vulnerabilities, with recall prioritised over precision.
Behavior gadget chains: chaining logical program behavior instead of vulnerabilities or primitives (credited to colleagues' talk).
Privilege escalation in OpenBMC IPMI by replacing a session's authorization context with a target account while keeping the original integrity and encryption keys.
defense: Rewrite a vulnerable function in a running app from log-detected attacks and bind the replacement to the running instances, with a way to return to the original code.
Track coverage of guards per finding shape, find shapes that rest on a single guard or have none, and alert on guard coverage regressions as an operational signal.
Treat the large pool of findings as a dataset for building the guard map rather than as a patch queue.
Encode threat intelligence as weighted hypothesis graphs (adversary brains) matched against telemetry, and use partially matched brains to drive collection of missing evidence.
takeaways: On the speaker's own model, with no data behind it, audit where your team's AI use sits among the four layers and pick one workflow to restructure at layer 3 or 4 rather than orchestrating it faster.
Pilot a guard inventory and guard-coverage regression alert on one codebase, using existing scanner output as input, before deciding whether patch volume is the right metric.
Treat model-generated leads from unconventional prompts (trust boundaries, symmetry) as recall-oriented inputs and budget a separate verification stage.
Experiment with hypothesis-style detection content next to Sigma and YARA, starting from your prose threat reports, but wait for evidence of detection quality before relying on it.
On the speaker's experience alone, re-run abandoned AI experiments whenever a new model ships.
limits: The self-healing demo is vibe coded and may not work in production.
He does not know whether the guard-based approach will scale.
Verification was deliberately skipped at the lead-generation stage.
The Adversary Brains preprint is not peer reviewed and he asks listeners not to judge it too harshly.
Code for Snouter and Code Surf was not yet released; he promises to release some.
critique: Nearly every claim is shown by demo or assertion; there are no precision, false-positive or detection-rate numbers for Snouter, Code Surf or Adversary Brains.
The 600+ results and 2,500 findings are raw counts with one confirmed defense-in-depth bug reported for the second, so the signal-to-noise of the tools is unknown.
The talk gives no breakdown of how much of the OpenBMC finding came from Snouter versus HD Moore's prior three months of work.

The jump from 2,500 findings on one hardened project to a general claim that defenders can maintain around 4,000 guards instead of 100,000 findings is not supported by data in the recording; the speaker says he does not know whether it will scale.

No testing of a wrong patch, attacker-triggered rewrites or absence of review was shown for live patching from log detection; the speaker described the demo as vibe coded and not necessarily production ready.

signal.reason: The talk presents several ideas (guard coverage regression, hypothesis-graph detections) with one published CVE, and the results shown are demos and stated assertions, with no measured detection or precision data.

The captions say 'Daniel Gashi and Tamir Isakhal' and 'my a byte'; the slide says Daniel Geyshis and Tamir Isaschar and BITE, and this record uses the slide.
Raptor is never defined in the talk, and this record uses the name as spoken.
The captions say Opus 4.8 and Opus 5; no slide shows either, and this record says only a newer Opus model.
